summary:
We developed Find my X, an open-source, interactive web platform and scientific pipeline built with FastAPI and Astropy to explore NASA's SPHEREx infrared all-sky survey (DR1 and QR3) and hunt for elusive celestial objects—including ultra-cool brown dwarfs, variable stars, and a hypothetical Planet X.

Addressing the "Planet X and SPHEREx" challenge, our platform retrieves real multi-epoch FITS cutouts from NASA/IPAC IRSA and resolves SPHEREx's Linear Variable Filter geometry by pairing wavelength-matched exposures, equalizing Point Spread Functions (PSF), and computing calibrated temporal subtractions. An automated AI/computer-vision engine detects moving dipoles and variable stars above 4-sigma, estimating both proper motion and heliocentric parallax distance in AU. Users can explore live blink comparators, shift-and-stack tracking, false-color infrared RGB composites, multi-mission historical timelines (DSS2, 2MASS, AllWISE, Gaia DR3, SPHEREx), 102-band spectra (0.75–5.00 µm) with Planck temperature fitting, and a bilingual 3D educational module.

This is vital because SPHEREx's vast spectral archives are complex to navigate; our tool transforms raw infrared telemetry into accessible, reproducible time-domain discovery for scientists and citizen astronomers alike.
details:
1. WHAT DOES IT DO AND HOW DOES IT WORK?

Find my X is an end-to-end scientific web platform and astronomical processing pipeline designed to analyze real multi-epoch infrared data from NASA's SPHEREx space telescope (Data Release 1 [DR1] and Quick Release 3 [QR3]) alongside legacy sky surveys. Users can enter any sky coordinate (RA, Dec, FoV in decimal or HMS/DMS format) or select from five official NASA test targets (WISE 0855, Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, RW Aurigae, and R Draconis) to perform time-domain and spectral discovery:

- Multi-Epoch Acquisition & LVF Wavelength Matching: Unlike conventional filter-wheel telescopes, SPHEREx uses Linear Variable Filters (LVF) across 6 detectors (D1–D6, 0.75 to 5.00 µm), meaning wavelength varies continuously with focal-plane position. Our backend queries NASA/IPAC IRSA via indexed SIA (`spherex_dr1` + `spherex_qr3`) and TAP (`spherex.artifact` + `spherex.plane`), evaluates the 2D spectral WCS (`WCS-WAVE`), and pairs exposures taken at different epochs only when their effective wavelengths match within strict physical tolerances (Δλ/λ ≤ 3%).

- WCS Reprojection, PSF Equalization & Calibrated Subtraction (ΔI): All cutouts are reprojected onto a common North-Up gnomonic TAN World Coordinate System (WCS) grid. Bitmask contamination flags (`FLAGS`) are filtered while preserving valid point-source bits (`MP_SOURCE`, `MP_FULLSAMPLE`). Before subtracting epochs (B − A), the pipeline performs Gaussian Point Spread Function (PSF) equalization and robust relative photometric scaling so static background stars cancel out without introducing false residuals.

- Automated AI / Computer Vision Anomaly Detector & Planet X Estimator: On the calibrated difference map (ΔI), our detection engine identifies statistically significant (>4σ) anomalies and classifies them into:

* Moving Dipoles (`MOVING_DIPOLE`): Negative-positive lobe pairs caused by sources that shifted position between epochs. The engine computes both linear proper motion (µ in arcsec/yr, testing the nearby brown dwarf/star hypothesis) and equivalent heliocentric parallax distance (d in AU, testing the trans-Neptunian object / Planet X hypothesis).

* Variable Monopoles (`VARIABLE_MONOPOLE`): Isolated flux surges or drops caused by young stellar objects or pulsating AGB variable stars.

- Interactive Visual Optics, Shift-and-Stack & False-Color RGB: In the browser, users can run a 1–6 FPS multi-epoch flipbook, a dedicated comparable Blink A/B mode, per-detector SNR median coadds (D1–D6), 60 FPS WiseView-style live pixel optics (Asinh/Linear transfer, contrast gain, B/W inversion on Float32Arrays), bilinear Shift-and-Stack motion tracking along (pmRA, pmDec) vectors to boost faint moving-object SNR by ~√N, and live 3-band infrared RGB false-color synthesis (<1.65 µm Blue, 1.65–3.0 µm Green, ≥3.0 µm Red).

- Multi-Decade Historical Timeline ("Línea Histórica") & 102-Band Spectroscopy: Clicking any source generates:

* A plain-language verdict ("This object moved between dates", "Brightness changed by X%", or "No measurable change") backed by 3σ statistical thresholds, a fixed-crosshair stamp strip spanning ~40 years (DSS2 ~1984–2000, 2MASS 1997–2001, AllWISE 2010–2011, and every SPHEREx 2025–2026 visit), centroid shift tracking, and a strict same-wavelength brightness curve.

* An on-the-fly 102-band infrared spectrum F(λ) in MJy/sr with `VARIANCE` error propagation, automated Planck blackbody temperature fitting (T_eff), molecular absorption band markers (H₂O, CH₄, CO), and 1-click CSV/PNG/WebM export.

- Interactive 3D Educational Module ("Learn in 3D"): A bilingual (English/Spanish) interactive 3D experience integrated with the landing page and explorer to visually explain SPHEREx hardware and celestial mechanics.

2. WHAT BENEFITS DOES IT HAVE?

- Eliminates False Positives in SPHEREx Time-Domain Analysis: Naive subtraction of SPHEREx images fails because different visits fall on different LVF wavelengths; our strict Δλ/λ ≤ 3% matching and PSF homogenization prevent color-gradient artifacts from masquerading as variable or moving objects.

- Zero-Latency Browser Optics & Offline Resilience: Pre-cached real FITS cutouts for all 5 official NASA benchmark targets load in ~1 second offline, while client-side `Float32Array` rendering enables 0 ms, 60 FPS contrast/stretch adjustments without server round-trips.

- Multi-Mission Contextualization in One Screen: Integrates SPHEREx with Gaia DR3 (including proper motion vectors), AllWISE, 2MASS, DSS2, SIMBAD, the NASA Exoplanet Archive, and Aladin Lite VOTable exports.

- Dual-Level Accessibility: Bridges rigorous astrophysics (MJy/sr aperture photometry, WCS-WAVE, variance propagation, VOTable/CSV export) with plain-language historical headlines and interactive 3D learning for students and citizen scientists.

3. WHAT IS THE INTENDED IMPACT OF THE PROJECT?

SPHEREx maps the entire sky every six months in 102 infrared bands, creating an unprecedented treasure trove for discovering cold, faint objects that are invisible in optical surveys—such as Y-type brown dwarfs (like WISE 0855 at ~250 K), free-floating planetary-mass objects, distant trans-Neptunian bodies, or a hypothetical Planet X. However, raw multi-extension FITS archives and spatially varying LVF wavelengths create a steep barrier to entry. Our project aims to democratize infrared time-domain astronomy—empowering both professional astronomers to rapidly vet transient and moving candidates, and citizen scientists worldwide (in the spirit of Backyard Worlds: Planet 9) to participate in genuine solar neighborhood discoveries.

4. WHAT TOOLS, CODING LANGUAGES, HARDWARE, OR SOFTWARE DID YOU USE?

- Backend & Scientific Pipeline: Python (3.10–3.14), FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pydantic v2, Astropy (FITS I/O, `WCS`, `WCS-WAVE` spectral lookup, `SkyCoord`, time transformations), NumPy, SciPy (Gaussian PSF convolution, signal/image processing, curve fitting, statistical hypothesis testing), Pandas, and PyVO (Virtual Observatory TAP/SIA protocols).

- Astronomical Data Sources & Protocols: NASA/IPAC IRSA SIA & TAP (`spherex_dr1`, `spherex_qr3`, `spherex.artifact`, `spherex.plane`), IRSA IBE (AllWISE, NEOWISE-R, 2MASS), ESA Gaia DR3 (via IRSA TAP, ARI Gaia, and CDS VizieR fallback), CDS SIMBAD, CDS `hips2fits` (gnomonic TAN projection cutouts), and NASA Exoplanet Archive.

- Frontend, Visualization & 3D: HTML5, CSS3 / Tailwind CSS, Vanilla JavaScript (ES6+, `Float32Array` pixel shaders on HTML5 Canvas, `MediaRecorder` for `.webm` video export), Plotly.js (interactive 102-band spectra with Planck blackbody curves and timeline light curves), Aladin Lite v3 (WebGL2 sky reference & VOTable export), and Three.js / WebGL for the bilingual "Learn in 3D" module and landing experience.

- Quality Assurance & Tooling: Python `unittest` suite (7 comprehensive test modules covering PSF subtraction, dipole/monopole classification, LVF wavelength pairing, timeline photometry, catalog fallbacks, and cross-platform launcher verification), Node.js verification scripts, Git, and Reducto (MCP code knowledge graph for codebase navigation). Developed and tested on standard consumer hardware (Windows/Linux/macOS PCs without requiring dedicated server GPUs).

5. HOW IS YOUR PROJECT CREATIVE?

- Solving the "Moving Filter" Paradox: Turning SPHEREx's Linear Variable Filters from a time-domain obstacle into a strength by combining strict iso-wavelength pairing (Δλ/λ ≤ 3%) for temporal subtraction with full 102-band spectral reconstruction on the exact same patch of sky.

- Dual-Hypothesis Astrometric Dipole Interpreter: Every detected moving dipole is simultaneously evaluated under two physical models—a nearby interstellar object (proper motion µ in arcsec/yr) and a bound outer Solar System body shifting via reflex parallax (heliocentric distance in AU for Planet X candidates).

- "Smart Aperture" Historical Timeline for High-Proper-Motion Stars: Fast-moving targets like Barnard's Star or WISE 0855 have moved 1.6' to 4.6' since their J2000/AllWISE catalog epochs. Instead of showing an empty crosshair in 2026 data, our timeline automatically computes the trajectory across 40 years of archival imagery (DSS2 -> 2MASS -> AllWISE -> SPHEREx), tracks the object with a moving photometric aperture, and provides a 1-click "Jump to current position" button.

- Client-Side Shift-and-Stack + Auto-Track AI Dipole: Bringing a professional heliospheric/astrometric technique directly into the browser canvas so users can align and stack multi-epoch frames along an AI-detected velocity vector in real time.

6. WHAT FACTORS DID YOUR TEAM CONSIDER?

- Scientific Rigor & Honest Uncertainty: We refused to mix incompatible wavelengths or invent detections on noisy data. If a target lacks strict iso-wavelength visits (Δλ/λ ≤ 3%), the system clearly labels any broader-band comparison as an "Approximate Estimate" and never claims variability unless p < 0.0027 (≥3σ) and amplitude ≥ 8%. Saturated cores (e.g., R Draconis, Barnard's Star) are handled via halo photometry and ring-centroiding.

- Service Reliability & Multi-Tier Fallbacks: External astronomical archives (IRSA TAP, CDS VizieR) can experience high latency or HTTP 503 bottlenecks. We engineered indexed SIA fast-paths (~1.5 s response), thread-safe semaphores, circuit-breakers, multi-mirror fallbacks (IRSA -> ARI Gaia -> Harvard VizieR -> CDS), and local disk caching so the user experience never breaks during live demos.

- Cross-Platform Reproducibility: We built a 1-click self-verifying launcher (`start_project.py` / `run_project.bat` / `run_project.sh`) that automatically provisions the virtual environment, verifies cached FITS integrity, and starts the platform on Windows, macOS, or Linux.
